teaser: A tax dispute painted into a church wall, and the moment painted people first seemed to have weight.
review_notes:
IMAGE IS A CROP: the file shows only the central group of the fresco (Christ, the apostles, the tax collector). The two side episodes (Peter at the lake on the left, Peter paying on the right) and the building are outside the image, so the lesson describes them in words only and never points at them.
Full fresco about 255 x 598 cm.
Painted in 32 giornate (figure commonly cited from the restoration reports).
Attribution of Christ's head to Masolino is a long-standing but debated hypothesis; presented as 'some specialists think'.
Masaccio born December 1401, died in Rome in 1428, aged 26. Nickname translation ('Big Tom' / 'Clumsy Tom') follows Vasari.
Torrigiano breaking Michelangelo's nose while they were drawing in the Carmine church: reported by Vasari and Cellini.
Fire of 1771 destroyed much of Santa Maria del Carmine; chapel cleaned in the 1980s.
Painted light matching the real chapel window (on the altar wall, to the right of this scene): standard observation, worth a check.
Year 1425 from metadata; usually dated c. 1425-1427.

lesson.text: You cannot hang this picture, crate it or lend it to another museum. It has no canvas and no frame. It is a skin of plaster a few millimeters thick, stuck to the stone of a chapel in Florence since the 1420s. To see it, you go to the wall.

The method is called fresco, Italian for “fresh.” The painter spreads a patch of wet plaster and paints on it before it dries, so the color sets inside the wall itself. Each patch is one day's work. What you see here is the middle of a scene nearly six meters wide (almost 20 feet).
Restorers can count the seams between the daily patches of plaster. The whole scene, with more than a dozen life-size figures, took Masaccio about 32 working days.

The story comes from the Gospel of Matthew. Jesus and his twelve apostles arrive in a town, and an official stops them: the temple tax is due. They have no money. Masaccio paints the second after the demand, when everyone turns to Jesus to see what he will do.
Twelve followers, one teacher, and one outsider who came to collect. He has no halo. Which one is he?

spots.title: The tax collector
spots.text: No halo, no long robe: a short orange tunic and bare legs, the street clothes of Masaccio's own Florence. He stands with his back to us, so we join the circle just behind his shoulder.

lesson.text: His turned back does a lot of work. The holy figures are wrapped in timeless cloaks, but the man asking for money looks like someone from 1425. For the first viewers, the Bible story had just walked into their own street.

Jesus answers with an odd instruction. Peter is to go to the lake, catch a fish, and open its mouth: a coin will be inside. Nobody in the picture speaks, of course. So how do you paint an order being given, doubted and passed along?
Follow the arms. Masaccio turns a conversation into a relay of hands.

lines.label: The order
lines.text: Christ's right arm stretches out to the left. It is the calm center of the picture, and every other gesture reacts to it.

lines.label: The echo
lines.text: Peter, gray-bearded in blue under a salmon-pink cloak, repeats the gesture with his own arm, as if asking “Over there? Me?” His hand points out of our view, toward the lake.

lines.label: The demand
lines.text: The collector's left arm swings the opposite way, to the right, toward the town where the tax must be paid. Two directions, one argument.

lesson.text: Those hands point at the rest of the wall. Beyond the left edge of this view, Peter crouches at the water with the fish. Beyond the right edge, he drops the coin into the collector's palm. One man appears three times in one picture, a device called continuous narrative: several moments of a story shown in a single scene.
Masaccio tells the story through bodies. A stretched arm, a frown and a turned back carry the plot, with no need for written words or symbols.

Now forget the story and notice how solid everyone is. A hundred years of Italian painting had loved gold backgrounds and slender, floating saints. These men are heavy. Their cloaks hang from real shoulders, their bare feet press the ground, and light strikes them from one side only, the right.
That light is no accident. The chapel's real window sits to the right of the scene, so the painted shadows fall the way real ones would. Daylight in the room and light in the picture agree.

The painter was about 24. His name was Tommaso, and Florence called him Masaccio, roughly “Big Tom” or “Clumsy Tom,” because he cared about painting and little else, including his clothes and his debts. He left for Rome soon after and died there in 1428, at 26.

spots.title: Christ
spots.text: The quietest face in the group. Some specialists think this gentle head was painted by Masolino, the older partner who shared the chapel job with Masaccio.

spots.title: Peter's frown
spots.text: Knitted brows, tight mouth, eyes fixed on Christ. Peter is not serene. He is a fisherman who has just been told to go find money inside a fish.

spots.title: Tilted haloes
spots.text: Older painters drew haloes as flat gold circles behind the head. Here they are discs seen at an angle, hovering above each skull like plates. Even holiness obeys the rules of space.

spots.title: The young apostle
spots.text: The blond, beardless one is traditionally John, the youngest. His smooth profile sits between two weathered, bearded heads: Masaccio varies ages and tempers like a casting director.

spots.title: Feet on the ground
spots.text: The collector's weight rests on one leg while the other heel lifts. Dark patches spread on the earth around the feet: cast shadows, still a rare sight in painting at this date.

spots.title: Bare hills
spots.text: No gold sky, no flowery meadow. Gray mountains and a few thin trees fade into pale air, so the group seems to stand in real weather.

lesson.text: Florence noticed. For generations, young artists climbed into this chapel with paper and chalk to copy the figures, the way music students learn a score. Leonardo, Raphael and Michelangelo are all said to have studied here.

Michelangelo carried a souvenir of those sessions for life. While they were drawing in this church, a fellow student named Pietro Torrigiano lost his temper and punched him, flattening his nose for good.

The wall has had a rough time since. In 1771 a fire gutted most of the church around it. The chapel survived, but smoke and old varnish left the scenes brown and dim for two centuries. A cleaning in the 1980s brought back the pinks, oranges and sea-greens you see here. They are still on the same wall, waiting for visitors to come to them.

quiz.question: What does “fresco” mean for how this work was made?
options: It was painted on fresh, wet plaster on the wall
It was painted in oil on a wooden panel
It was woven and then glued to the wall
quiz.explanation: Fresco means painting on fresh plaster, so the color sets inside the wall.

quiz.question: How can you tell the tax collector from the apostles?
options: He holds a bag of coins
He has no halo and wears a short tunic
quiz.explanation: He is the only man without a halo, dressed like a Florentine of the 1420s.

quiz.question: Where does Jesus tell Peter the coin will be found?
options: In the mouth of a fish
quiz.explanation: Peter is sent to the lake to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth.

quiz.question: What is “continuous narrative”?
options: A painting that covers a whole room
A story told in a series of separate framed panels
Several moments of one story shown in a single scene
quiz.explanation: In the full fresco Peter appears three times, at three moments of the story.

quiz.question: Why does the painted light come from the right?
options: It matches the chapel's real window
The right side stands for heaven
The left side of the wall was damaged
quiz.explanation: Masaccio matched his painted light to the daylight entering the chapel.

facts.text: Masaccio lived to old age and spent decades finishing this chapel.
facts.explanation: He died in Rome in 1428, aged 26.

facts.text: The haloes in this scene are drawn as discs seen at an angle.
facts.explanation: They tilt in space above the heads instead of sitting flat behind them.

facts.text: The scene was painted on canvas and later glued to the chapel wall.
facts.explanation: It is a fresco, painted directly into wet plaster on the wall.
